reasoning: Failure edits were kept in full. Success edits were kept where they cover patterns the failure edits do not: quoted-lyric titles, proverb pronouns, definition/etymology headwords, quiz-forum replies, 'X & this person' and 'others called him this' clues, species names, and glued letter counts. The two person-name edits overlap, so I merged the success edit's points (no titles or descriptors, no shrinking to a first name or bare surname without an archive line) into the failure edit and kept it as failure-sourced. I moved some anchors to the end of their bullets so inserts do not split a bullet: the 'never shorten a verbatim answer' edit now follows 'Before the answer tags, briefly quote the matched line.', and the quoted-lyric edit follows the real-people list bullet. The second move also avoids two inserts on the same Conch target. No edit touches the protected SLOW_UPDATE section.

edits.target: Before the answer tags, briefly quote the matched line.
edits.content: - Never SHORTEN a verbatim archive answer either. Rule 4's delete-clue-words and bare-noun trimming do NOT apply to it. Copy the text after the final '|' exactly as printed, keeping a leading 'a/an/the' and any generic noun even if the clue already says that word ('...this Australian gum tree that reaches 300 feet | a eucalyptus tree' -> 'a eucalyptus tree', not 'Eucalyptus').

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- Pronoun and possessive clues: the answer is what the pronoun stands for, never an anchor inside the clue.
  - Thing or category: 'They were once called "Saratoga Chips" after the town where they were first made' / 'It was nicknamed X' -> the thing that bore the quoted name ('Potato chips'), not the place ('Saratoga Springs'). For 'they/these' the answer is usually a plural or mass-noun category.
  - Person: 'Her home in Rochester is now a museum...' / 'His 1925 novel...' -> the PERSON ('Susan B. Anthony', not 'Susan B. Anthony Museum & House'), not the house, museum, book or institution the passages name.
- Class check: the answer must belong to the class the clue's noun names. 'this very caustic acid' needs an ACID ('hydrochloric acid'), not a base such as NaOH or lye, even if most passages discuss the base. Keep the word 'acid', because bare 'hydrochloric' is incomplete. 'this vitamin' -> 'C' alone, never 'vitamin C'.

edits.target: and answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content:
- Foreign-word clues ('This, an orzel in Poland, is seen on our coins'): the clue gives the foreign word as a gloss, so answer with its English meaning ('eagle'), never the foreign word itself.
- Description clues with no 'this' ('A house with floors that differ by about half a story') ask for the standard NAME of the thing described ('split-level'). Do not restate the description's own words or numbers ('1.5 story'). Look in the passages for the term that glosses that description (e.g. 'split-level entry ... raised half a storey').

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Person-name form: (a) if a verbatim archive line gives a bare surname or short form ('... of "The Maids" | Genet.'), the answer is exactly that ('Genet'), not an expanded 'Jean Genet'. Copy the archived form, even when it is shorter than a full name. (b) Without a verbatim hit, give the plain 'First Last' form a trivia key would list, as the passages repeat it ('Joel Chandler Harris', 'Jessica Savitch', 'Marilyn Monroe'). Never use the encyclopedia headline form with extra middle names, suffixes or a nickname in quotes ('Marion Barry', not 'Marion Shepilov Barry, Jr.'; 'Tony Williams', not 'Anthony Allen "Tony" Williams'). Do not add titles, roles or descriptors, and do not shrink the name to a first name or bare surname unless an archive line shows that form.

edits.target: Never cut a part that identifies the person: keep the regnal numeral of a king or of a play's title character ('Richard III', not 'Richard'; 'Henry V').
edits.content: - Branch/campus/location qualifiers: when the clue itself supplies the campus, city or branch ('this state university at Superior, not Madison'), strike it from the answer name and give the parent institution or organisation: 'University of Wisconsin', not 'University of Wisconsin-Superior'. This is the delete-clue-words test applied to hyphenated or suffixed qualifiers.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content:
- Mixed or noisy passages: when the context blends several people or countries (a Hall of Fame class page, a vote that admitted one government and expelled another), do NOT pick the most-mentioned name. Anchor on the clue's UNIQUE details: team or organization, career length, exact stats ('Brewers, 20 years, 3,142 hits' -> the player whose own stat line carries those numbers, not another player on the same page), size descriptors ('population giant' -> China, not Taiwan), and direction verbs (admitted or joined vs lost, expelled or out). Re-read the passage line holding the clue's exact numbers or verb and check whose name sits with it.
- Role-plus-event person clues ('His 2-week sabbatical as mayor of Washington, D.C. made headlines'): the distinctive event or trait identifies the person, because the role is shared by many holders. Do NOT choose a person just because a passage title matches the role, or because he is the best-documented or most recent holder. Check which candidate the passages tie to the event. If no passage does, use your own knowledge of who is famous for that episode, and prefer a candidate whose own page is among the retrieved passages and fits the era.

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content: - Quoted lyric or line clues ('1991 hit that contains the lines "I thought that I heard you laughing..."') ask for the TITLE of the song, poem or speech that contains the quote, not the artist, the album or the lyric itself. Find the passages that repeat the quoted words next to a title (songfacts, lyrics pages, 'Album=... Song Lyrics') and use the year or 'hit' detail to confirm. Give the bare title without quotation marks ('Losing My Religion').

edits.target: When passages are noisy, use your own knowledge of sports terms and idioms.
edits.content: - Proverb, saying or quotation clues with a pronoun ('Its mother is necessity', 'It begins at home'): the pronoun is the hidden answer. Complete the saying (necessity is the mother of invention) and answer with the noun the pronoun stands for ('Invention'). Do not answer with a word already in the quote.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - Definition, term or etymology clues ('referred to by this term', 'this unit is equal to...', 'This adjective ... comes from the Latin for "before behind"'): look for the dictionary, glossary or etymology line that paraphrases the clue or quotes its literal gloss ('Apogee: the farthest point from the Earth in the Moon's orbit'; 'Man-hours: an industrial unit equal to the work one person can do in an hour'; 'literally "before-behind"'). The headword being defined, often in a page title or shared by several entries, is the answer. Copy it in singular dictionary form ('Man-hour', 'Apogee', 'preposterous') and keep the part of speech the clue names. Do not answer with the Latin or Greek root or a synonym.

edits.target: Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content: - When the context is only a few short snippets that repeat the clue (quiz-archive listings, forum posts), a reply posted right beside the verbatim clue ('Alex, is that INVENTION?', 'the answer is X') is the best evidence. Use it when no explicit archive answer contradicts it and it fits the clue's wording. Give the answer in the word form the poster used, minus 'What is' / 'Who is'.

edits.target: asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content:
- 'X & this <actor/person>' ('Lemmon & this actor joined an all-girl band', 'Laurel & this comedian'): X is an anchor already given. The answer is the OTHER member of the pair or group. Take the co-star or partner the passages list with X in the same sentence or cast line ('Tony Curtis and Jack Lemmon'). Do not repeat X, and do not answer with the film, the character or the group name.
- 'His/her name was X, but others called him this' / 'known to most as this': the answer is the OTHER name, title or role the passages give the character ('Zeb' -> 'Grandpa'). Never repeat the name already in the clue, and do not stretch the answer with a surname or extra words ('Grandpa Walton').

edits.target: The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content: - Species and varieties: for 'this bird / this tree / this animal' where the passages consistently use one standard (often 'official state') name with its qualifier ('the Brown Pelican is Louisiana's state bird'), answer with that full standard name ('Brown Pelican'). Only the bare category word ('bird') is dropped; the qualifier is part of the name, not an echo of the clue.

edits.target: If a bare number appears in parentheses, treat it only as this hint, not as part of the question.
edits.content: - The count may be glued to the clue with no space ('He spun straw into gold(15)'). Use it as a check on your candidate (Rumpelstiltskin = 15 letters), and keep it out of the answer tags.
